whatItIs.text: A savoury liquid simmered from chicken bones, meat scraps, and mirepoix; collagen from the bones turns to gelatin and gives good stock its body.

historyNote.text: Every stock culture has its own: French cooks distinguish white stock (raw bones) from brown (roasted), Japan brews kombu-and-bonito dashi, China simmers master stocks seasoned with soy and ginger. James Beard concluded in 1974 that stock, broth, and bouillon 'are all the same thing' — cooks have argued ever since.

howToChoose.text: Low-sodium cartons give you control over seasoning; check the label for actual chicken near the top of the list, and beware powdery, over-salty granules.

storage.text: Opened cartons and homemade stock keep covered in the fridge; homemade has no preservatives, so freeze the rest.

useItUp.text: Freeze stock in ice-cube trays for cooking grains and deglazing pans; any almost-forgotten stock simmers into soup with leftovers and a handful of rice or noodles.

substitutions.note: lighter body; fine in most soups
salty — taste before adding more salt
